# Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (TEST FIXTURE — not clinical content)

**Pathophysiology**
Absolute or relative insulin deficiency drives ketone production and osmotic diuresis.
- Insulin deficiency with raised counter-regulatory hormones increases hepatic glucose output and lipolysis. [1]
- Free fatty acids are converted to ketone bodies, causing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
- Osmotic diuresis causes volume depletion and electrolyte loss, including total body potassium.
- Potassium shifts out of cells in acidosis, so serum potassium can look normal while stores are depleted.

## Signs & Symptoms
**Symptoms:**
- Polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain.
- Drowsiness or confusion in severe cases.

**Examination signs:**
- Dehydration with tachycardia and hypotension.
- Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath.

**Red flags:**
- Reduced Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, shock, or serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L.

**Precipitants:**
- Infection, missed insulin doses, new-onset type 1 diabetes, myocardial infarction.

### Differentials
| Condition | Key separating feature |
|---|---|
| Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state | Glucose usually very high with little ketosis |
| Alcoholic ketoacidosis | Alcohol history, glucose normal or low |

## Investigations
### Diagnostic criteria
| Criterion | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Capillary or plasma glucose | Above 11.0 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or known diabetes |
| Ketones | β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or above |
| Acidosis | Venous pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L |

### Bedside and bloods
| Test | Normal (adult) | In this condition | What it means / next step | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capillary β-hydroxybutyrate | Below 0.6 mmol/L | 3.0 mmol/L or above | Confirms ketoacidosis; target fall of 0.5 mmol/L per hour | [1] Table 2 |
| Venous pH | 7.35–7.45 | Below 7.30 | Severity marker; repeat every 1–2 hours | [1] Table 2 |
| Serum potassium | 3.5–5.0 mmol/L | Variable, often high on admission | Replace if below 5.5 mmol/L once urine output is confirmed | [2] Section 4 |
| Serum creatinine | 60–110 µmol/L (0.7–1.2 mg/dL) | Raised in volume depletion | Guides fluids and drug dosing | [2] Section 4 |
| 12-lead Electrocardiogram (ECG) | Normal sinus rhythm | Peaked T waves or arrhythmia with potassium disturbance | Start cardiac monitoring if abnormal | [2] Section 4 |

### Imaging and specialist
| Test | Normal (adult) | In this condition | What it means / next step | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chest X-ray | Clear lung fields | Consolidation if infection precipitated DKA | Treat the precipitant | [2] Section 5 |
| Computed Tomography (CT) abdomen | No acute pathology | Intra-abdominal source in selected patients | Image only if examination suggests a surgical cause | [2] Section 5 |

## Management
### Immediate (0–60 minutes)
- Give 0.9% sodium chloride 1000 mL intravenously over the first hour in Emergency Department (ED) patients without heart failure.
- Start fixed-rate intravenous insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour after fluids have started.
- Monitor capillary glucose and ketones hourly.

### Ongoing (1–24 hours)
- Add 5% glucose when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L (250 mg/dL).
- Replace potassium to keep the level at 4.0–5.5 mmol/L.

### Escalation
- Call Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for GCS below 12, pH below 7.0, or potassium below 3.5 mmol/L.

### Medicines
| Drug | Indication | Patient group | Dose | Route | Frequency | Duration / maximum | Adjustments | Monitoring | Contraindications / cautions | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Soluble insulin | Reverse ketogenesis | Adults | 0.1 units/kg/hour | IV infusion | Continuous | Until ketones below 0.6 mmol/L | Reduce rate if glucose falls faster than 3 mmol/L per hour; Check hospital formulary | Glucose and ketones hourly; potassium 2-hourly | Hypokalaemia below 3.5 mmol/L until corrected; Hypersensitivity | [1] Table 4 |

### Discharge criteria
- Ketones below 0.6 mmol/L, pH above 7.30 and eating normally.

### Follow-up
- Diabetes specialist review within 1 week.

### Patient education
- Sick-day rules and when to seek help.

### Lifestyle and diet
- Carbohydrate counting and regular glucose monitoring.

### Team referrals
- Diabetes specialist team on the day of admission.

### Learning objectives
- Recognise and stage diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

### Key points
- Fluids first, then insulin; correct potassium before insulin if below 3.5 mmol/L.

### Pitfalls
- Stopping the insulin infusion when glucose normalises but ketones remain raised.
